lines.text: Childcare.
Often both parents work.

Childcare can be arranged in different ways: a babysitter [oppas] — for example grandpa or grandma, a host parent [gastouder] — someone at whose home several children are looked after, or a daycare centre [kinderdagverblijf].
From the age of four, a child can go after school hours to after-school care [buitenschoolse opvang, BSO].
School for toddlers.
When a child is two or two and a half years old, he may go to toddler care [peuteropvang], formerly known as peuterspeelzaal.
That is a school for children up to four years old, two or three times a week for a few hours.
Toddlers learn to speak Dutch better there, play together, and sing songs.
The pre-school [voorschool] is also a kind of toddler care; this is also called voorschoolse educatie or vve (voor- en vroegschoolse educatie).
The voorschool is for children with a developmental delay [achterstand], for example in the Dutch language.
Children from two to four years old go to the voorschool sixteen hours per week.
Primary school.
Children from four to about twelve years old go to primary school [basisschool].
Parents must register [aanmelden] their child; in most municipalities this can be done when a child is two and a half or three years old.
Parents can choose a school themselves, but there is not always a place.
There are eight groups.
Groups 1 and 2 contain young children of four and five years old [kleuters]; they are still allowed to play a lot.
In groups 3 through 8, the most important subjects [vakken] are Dutch language and arithmetic.
Secondary education [voortgezet onderwijs] (also called the middelbare school) begins when children are about twelve years old.
There are three levels:
The vwo lasts six years and is the most theory-focused [theorie].
After the vwo you can follow academic education [wo, wetenschappelijk onderwijs] at the universiteit — for professions such as doctor or lawyer [advocaat].
The havo lasts five years.
After that you can go to higher professional education [hbo, hoger beroepsonderwijs] — for professions such as teacher or physiotherapist.
The vmbo lasts four years and is the most practice-focused [praktijk].
After that you can go to secondary vocational education [mbo, middelbaar beroepsonderwijs] — for a practical profession, for example cook or mechanic.
Vmbo and mbo also have different levels of their own (mbo 1 through 4).
Which level suits the child?

The primary school teacher [leraar van de basisschool] gives a recommendation [advies] about the level — so parents may not choose the level themselves, but they may choose a school (that matches the level).
Children first enter the bridge class [brugklas]: the first year and sometimes also the second.
There they can usually still change level.
Moving up [Doorstromen].
With a diploma you can often continue studying at a higher level; sometimes your grades must be high enough.
For example: after mbo level 4 (the highest mbo level, such as teaching assistant) you can do an hbo programme to become a teacher.
Schakelklas.
Children who have not been in the Netherlands very long can go to a transition class [schakelklas]: children between four and twelve years old get extra language education there.
The ISK (internationale schakelklas) is for children from twelve years old; they attend the ISK for about two years.
Special care.
Children with behavioural problems [gedragsproblemen] or learning problems [leerproblemen] can get extra help at the regular school.
For children with more serious problems (a handicap or disorder), there are special schools [speciale scholen].
The school advises the parents.
Finding information: on the internet (every school has a website), asking people you know for advice, and visiting a school before you decide.
